newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Cyprus envoy said not seeking reappointment.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Cyprus envoy said not seeking reappointment.

text.p: Former South Korean Foreign Minister Han Sung-joo will not seek an extension of his appointment as U.N. special representative for Cyprus after completing a year in the post on April 30, a source at the United Nations said on Friday.
Han is due in Cyprus on Saturday on his latest visit to the divided island.

He is reported to have told Secretary-General Kofi Annan that, because of the quickening pace of U.N. diplomacy over Cyprus, it would be preferable to appoint someone who could devote more time to the problem.
Han, who was South Korea's foreign minister from February 1993 to December 1994, is professor of political science at Korea University.
He has visited Cyprus several times in the past year but is not permanently stationed there. The resident U.N. representative is Gustave Feissel.

The United Nations is trying to arrange talks before the end of June between President Glafcos Clerides, as head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash. It would be their first face to face encounter in nearly three years.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since 1974 when troops from Turkey took over the north of the island after a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The United Nations has been trying for decades to reunite Cyprus under a federal system.
The latest burst of diplomatic activity has been spurred by Cypriot hopes of joining the European Union. Membership talks would be greatly eased if the division of the island were ended.
Another reason for stepped up diplomatic efforts is what the United Nations regards as the dangerous militarization of Cyprus.
The internationally-recognised Greek Cypriot government has been upgrading its weaponry and earlier this year announced plans to buy S-300 surface-to-air missiles from Russia.

Turkey, which said it would do whatever was needed to prevent the scheduled deployment of the missiles next year, still has more than 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus, where a Turkish Cypriot state was proclaimed in 1983 but is recognised only by Ankara.
A U.N. force now comprising 1,200 troops has been stationed in Cyprus since 1964 and patrols a buffer zone across the island.
